report:
## Conclusion: The claim that soursop cures cancer in humans is not supported by scientific evidence.

Laboratory (in vitro) and animal studies suggest that compounds in soursop (graviola) can kill various cancer cell lines, including breast, prostate, colon, pancreatic, and liver cancers. However, **no human clinical trials** have demonstrated that soursop treats or cures cancer. Multiple authoritative sources confirm this gap:

- Cancer Research UK notes that while one mouse study showed a beneficial effect on prostate cancer cells, "there haven't been human studies, so we don't know whether it can work as a cancer treatment or not" ([PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/)).
- Wikipedia states soursop "is widely promoted as an alternative cancer treatment, but there is not enough reliable medical evidence that it is effective for treating cancer or any disease" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop)).
- MD Anderson Cancer Center confirms: "Soursop hasn't been shown to treat cancer in humans" ([MD Anderson](https://www.mdanderson.org/cancerwise/soursop-does-this-tropical-fruit-have-health-benefits.h00-159852978.html)).
- Experts also warn of safety risks, including potential interference with chemotherapy drugs, disruption of blood sugar metabolism during imaging tests, and neurological concerns ([Northwell](https://thewell.northwell.edu/chronic-diseases-conditions/soursop-cancer); [Advance Study](https://advancestudy.org/does-soursop-kill-cancer-cells/)).

**Bottom line:** Soursop shows interesting anticancer activity in lab settings, but there is no clinical evidence it cures cancer in humans. Relying on it as a substitute for proven cancer treatment could be dangerous.
